## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{17}{17}{17}{17}{16}{16}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can a model that proposes a useful action still fail to complete the task?_

A proposed repair can be correct while the surrounding system applies it to the wrong files, loses its progress, or stops before checking the result. Delegating a task therefore requires more than choosing a capable model. The system must decide what each call can see, which actions may execute, what state must survive, and what evidence supports acceptance. These responsibilities carry costs, but omitting them can leave the task unfinished or its effects outside the intended scope. A dependable design matches those responsibilities to the task rather than treating every demonstration as a complete system. The necessary machinery depends on how long execution continues, what state it carries, and how much authority it holds over the environment.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain how model proposals, authorized actions, and observations form a task trajectory
- Specify a task contract that separates the goal, environment, permitted actions, observations, and completion criteria
- Apply horizon, state, and authority to identify the engineering obligations of a delegated task
- Distinguish enforced boundaries from evidence supporting a task's acceptance
- Assign context, execution, and supervisory responsibilities to the components surrounding a foundation model
- Evaluate when model-directed decisions justify their added cost over a fixed workflow

:::

## The Agent's Existence Moment {#sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment}

A software engineering task asks for a repair to an intermittent race condition in a distributed key-value store. A foundation model can propose a change to the connection-pool locking logic, but the proposed patch leaves the repository untouched. Someone must inspect the relevant files, apply the change, run the compiler and tests, and decide whether the result satisfies the task. In a conversational interface, a human performs this work and returns selected observations to the model. In an agentic system, software coordinates these steps under delegated authority.

The agent's existence moment occurs when the system closes this interaction loop. A model receives the task and available observations, proposes a next step, and receives feedback from its execution. The surrounding software, the **runtime**\index{Runtime (agent)!definition} (often called the harness), decides whether the proposed action is permitted and dispatches it through a tool. A **tool**\index{Tool!definition} is an interface to an operation in the environment, such as reading a file, applying a patch, or running a test. Permission stays with the runtime; generating the name of an operation grants the model nothing. @Fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control contrasts the two ways the repair loop can close.

::: {#fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop**: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model's proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model's own report." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A, A Person Closes the Loop: a developer sends a prompt to a model endpoint and receives a patch, executes it in a local terminal, and re-pastes a compiler error to the endpoint along a dashed arrow. Panel B, A Runtime Closes the Loop: an agent runtime labeled authorizes each action sends context to a foundation model labeled holds no authority and receives a proposal, dispatches to an isolated sandbox that returns an observation, and the sandbox feeds verifiers whose evidence returns to the runtime along a dashed arrow."}
![](images/svg/open_vs_closed_loop_control.svg)
:::

Panel B is the arrangement this book engineers, and it needs a precise name.

::: {#dfn-vol3-agentic-system .callout-definition title="Agentic system"}

***Agentic system***\index{Agentic system!definition} is a software system in which a runtime places a foundation model in a loop with context, tools, and an environment, dispatching the model's authorized proposals and returning their observations to the next call until the task is accepted, stopped, or escalated.

1.  **Significance**: The unit of reliability and cost moves from the call to the task. Unchecked errors compound with the number of turns (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic), and every attempt, rejected or accepted, is charged to the task's cost per accepted result.
2.  **Distinction**: In a conversational interface a person runs the tools and carries each result back; in an agentic system the runtime closes the loop and holds the authority, so the model's output is only ever a proposal.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating agency as a model capability. A stronger model makes better proposals, but permission, preserved state, and the acceptance decision belong to the surrounding system.

:::

Following the repair task exposes how proposals, effects, and observations interact across turns. Execution begins when the runtime prepares a working copy of the repository and supplies the task description. The model proposes running the failing test. After authorizing that operation, the runtime invokes the test runner and records its result. When the test reports a deadlock, the runtime supplies the diagnostic output to the next model call, which proposes inspecting the connection-pool implementation. The returned source reveals the locking logic on which a repair must operate.

Guided by this inspection, the model proposes a patch. The runtime checks that the edit targets permitted files before applying it to the working copy. This step separates three things the runtime must track: the generated patch is a proposal, the changed file is an effect, and the tool's report of that change is an observation. When a compilation attempt reports an unclosed bracket, that observation changes the next decision. The model proposes a corrected patch, and the runtime applies it and reruns the checks. Once the compiler and visible tests pass, the runtime gathers the additional regression evidence required for acceptance, using tests the editing tools cannot modify, and records the deliverable together with the check results. If those results meet the task's stated acceptance standard, the runtime can submit the repair for acceptance; otherwise, the task continues, stops, or escalates.

The changing observations determine which steps are useful. A deadlock trace calls for different work than a syntax error, and a successful compilation does not establish that a race condition has disappeared. Even a regression test can miss an execution schedule that triggers the defect. The system therefore needs both a way to act on new evidence and a rule for deciding when the evidence is sufficient.

Closing a feedback loop is not new to computing. Feedback control and reinforcement learning already organize action around observations of an environment [@wiener1960; @sutton2018reinforcement]. Foundation-model agents use learned representations of language and code to propose actions in software environments; work such as ReAct demonstrates this interleaving of generated reasoning, actions, and observations [@yao2023react]. The engineering problem here is how to make that interleaving accountable. Fault isolation, access control, and recovery remain useful precisely because a generated proposal can be wrong.

### The trajectory as the systems management boundary {#sec-vol3-intro-trajectory-systems-boundary}

The accepted patch is only the final artifact of the repair. To understand how the system obtained it, we also need the failed compilation, the observations that led to the correction, the actions the runtime permitted, and the checks used to accept the result. The object that holds all of these is the book's unit of engineering.

::: {#dfn-vol3-trajectory .callout-definition title="Trajectory"}

***Trajectory***\index{Trajectory!definition} is the ordered sequence of recorded states, proposed actions, runtime decisions, and observations through which one delegated task proceeds, from its first context to its acceptance, stop, or escalation.

1.  **Significance**: The trajectory's length is the horizon $H$ that sets unchecked reliability, and its full span, including failed attempts, is the accounting boundary for cost per accepted task.
2.  **Distinction**: A transcript records what the model read and wrote. A trajectory also records which proposals the runtime rejected, dispatched, or completed and what the environment reported, so it connects each decision to the evidence available at the time.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Keeping only the final deliverable. The accepted patch alone hides the cost of the attempts that failed and the evidence on which acceptance rested.

:::

The compact notation

$$\tau = (s_0, a_0, o_1, s_1, a_1, o_2, \dots, s_T)$$

represents this sequence. Here, $s_t$ is the recorded state available at a decision step, $a_t$ is a candidate action, and $o_{t+1}$ is the subsequent observation. Each step from $s_t$ to $s_{t+1}$ is a **turn**\index{Turn!definition}: one model call and the runtime's handling of the action it proposes. The runtime's record must also mark whether it rejected, dispatched, or completed each proposed action. A rejected proposal has no effect, while a dispatched one whose response never arrived has an unknown effect, because the tool may have acted before the reply was lost. The notation fixes the order of the interaction, and $s_t$ is the runtime's recorded view, a partial picture of the environment.

The trajectory is the systems management boundary because dependencies cross individual calls. The corrected patch depends on a compiler result from an earlier turn. Each edit must remain within the task's current permissions, and the cost of the failed attempt still belongs to the task. A model request ends when its response returns; the delegated work, and any tool operation still outstanding, ends only when the runtime settles it. The system therefore decides, per task, which state and resources the continuing work still needs.

This boundary is why infrastructure built for independent requests cannot host a trajectory unchanged. Each assumption that makes a stateless service simple fails in a specific way once work spans turns, and each failure motivates a later part of the book. @Tbl-vol3-request-vs-trajectory pairs the request assumption with the trajectory's requirement and the chapter that owns the response.

| Concern       | Stateless request assumption                 | Trajectory requirement                                                                | Developed in                                             |
|:--------------|:---------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| **Cost**      | Each call has a bounded, independent cost    | Cost accumulates across turns and includes failed attempts                            | @sec-vol3-context-engineering, @sec-vol3-agent-economics |
| **Memory**    | State is discarded when the response returns | Context, serving state, and the workspace must survive between turns                  | @sec-vol3-kv-cache, @sec-vol3-long-term-memory           |
| **Authority** | A credential is granted to the whole service | Each action is checked against a grant scoped to the task                             | @sec-vol3-tool-calling, @sec-vol3-sandboxes              |
| **Recovery**  | A failed request can be retried              | Repeating an effect can duplicate it; recovery may require compensation               | @sec-vol3-durable-execution, @sec-vol3-failure-recovery  |
| **Evidence**  | A success status ends the request            | A success status is one observation; acceptance needs an independent check            | @sec-vol3-evaluation                                     |
| **Placement** | Any replica can serve any request            | Later turns benefit from reaching the retained serving state and the task's workspace | @sec-vol3-kv-cache                                       |
: **Request Assumptions That a Trajectory Breaks**: Each row names a simplification that stateless services rely on, the requirement a multi-turn task places in its stead, and where the book develops the response. {#tbl-vol3-request-vs-trajectory tbl-colwidths="[12,28,36,24]"}

An implementation can express the interaction as a short loop. The missing responsibilities become visible in @lst-vol3-naive-agent-loop, which dispatches whatever command it extracts from a model response and treats the response's completion marker as sufficient reason to stop. The listing is a failure example, not a recommended execution pattern.

::: {#lst-vol3-naive-agent-loop lst-cap="**An Unmediated Agent Loop**: Direct command dispatch and model-declared completion leave authority, task evidence, resource limits, and recovery unspecified."}
```python
prompt = task_description
while True:
    response = generate(prompt)
    command = parse_command(response)
    output = run_with_host_permissions(command)
    prompt += format_observation(command, output)
    if "TASK_COMPLETE" in response:
        break
```
:::

Suppose the first test fails and the model next proposes searching the entire host filesystem for the suspected function. Nothing in this loop restricts the search to the repository. Dispatch inherits the host process's permissions, although the repair needs only a much narrower set of operations. Whatever the search returns is appended to the prompt without a size limit or a decision about relevance. The next call must process that accumulated text, and an oversized history can exceed the model interface's input limit. These failures arise from omitted authorization and context management, not from the use of a loop itself.

The same implementation has no task-wide stopping rule beyond the completion marker. Repeatedly generating a slightly different repair can consume resources without resolving the failure. If the host process stops after applying a patch but before recording its result, the prompt disappears while the file change may remain. Restarting from the initial prompt can then act on a different repository state than the one that produced the original decision. Persistence and recovery requirements depend on whether that workspace is disposable and whether effects reach beyond it; the loop has made neither choice explicit.

These are familiar software-systems responsibilities applied at the lifetime of a delegated task. A short, disposable experiment need not use the same recovery machinery as a task that changes shared infrastructure. Both still need an explicit owner for permissions, retained state, and the decision to stop. Their implementation belongs outside the model's generated account of what it has done.

### Plausible output is not completion evidence {#sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible}

The repair loop can terminate with a fluent report even when the repository remains broken. A generated command can be syntactically valid yet target the wrong file; a test process can exit successfully because the proposed patch removed the failing assertion. This failure pattern is a **fail-plausible fault**\index{Fail-plausible fault!definition}: the output appears well formed and credible while the intended property remains unsatisfied.

The classical fault models show why this pattern needs a name. A fail-stop component halts when it faults, so a supervisor detects the failure by the missing progress or the error it raises [@schlichting1983failstop]. A Byzantine component may behave arbitrarily, and tolerating it requires replication and agreement among independent replicas [@lamport1982byzantine].[^fn-failstop-byzantine-faults] Plausible output defeats the first defense because nothing halts, and it passes shallow monitors such as exit status and syntax checks; repeated samples from the same model are not independent replicas, because they can share the same mistake. The term names the case the supervisor must anticipate; formally it is a special case of arbitrary failure, one that is shaped to look like success.

[^fn-failstop-byzantine-faults]: **Fail-Stop and Byzantine Faults**: Schlichting and Schneider defined a fail-stop processor as one that halts on failure without first making an erroneous state transition, so that other processors can detect the halt [@schlichting1983failstop]. Lamport, Shostak, and Pease showed that reaching agreement when some components may send arbitrary, conflicting messages requires more than two-thirds of the components to be correct, the origin of the $3f+1$ replica bound for tolerating $f$ such faults [@lamport1982byzantine]. \index{Fault model!fail-stop}\index{Fault model!Byzantine}

The model operates under **zero ambient authority**\index{Zero ambient authority!definition} in the architecture developed here: it holds no standing permission of its own, and every effect it causes passes through a grant the runtime checks. Its output cannot grant permission to execute a command, alter the runtime's record, or declare acceptance. The runtime must obtain evidence about the environment through designated tools and checks. For our repair, that means distinguishing the patch text from the applied diff and distinguishing a model-written summary of the test run from the actual test result.

Each external check establishes a specific claim, narrower than the task. A successful compilation establishes that the compiler accepted the program under its configuration; a passing regression test records what happened for the cases and schedules it exercised. Testing can expose defects without proving their absence\index{Verification!testing vs. proof} [@dijkstra1970structured].

Agency therefore belongs to the complete system that proposes, authorizes, acts, and assesses results. The trajectory makes those responsibilities visible across the repair, including unsuccessful attempts and uncertain outcomes. Before deciding which responsibilities a task needs, the engineer needs two numbers about its trajectory: how likely it is to finish correctly, and what each accepted result costs.

## Reliability and Cost over a Horizon {#sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic}

The repair trajectory runs for tens of turns, and each turn builds on the last. A misread deadlock trace sends the next call to the wrong file, and a patch to the wrong file repairs a different defect. Nothing in the model's output marks the turn where the trajectory went wrong, so a long task can fail even when almost every step is sound. Elementary probability shows how quickly. Suppose each of $H$ sequential steps is correct with probability $1-\epsilon$, errors are independent, and nothing checks a step before the next one builds on it. The task then succeeds only if every step does, with probability

$$\Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\epsilon)^{H}$$ {#eq-vol3-horizon-compounding}

@Eq-vol3-horizon-compounding is the series-reliability formula for components that must all work, applied to the turns of a trajectory; we call the resulting decay **horizon compounding**\index{Horizon compounding!definition}. Independence is a simplification. Correlated errors and partial recovery change the value, and the exponential dependence on the horizon remains (notebook \ref{nbk-01-horizon-compounding}).

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-intro-horizon-compounding
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HORIZON COMPOUNDING FOR UNCHECKED STEPS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding and @nbk-01-horizon-compounding.
# │ Goal: Show task success falling with horizon at a fixed step accuracy.
# │ Show: Success at two horizons; step error and eps*H needed for a target.
# │ How:  (1 - eps)^H with independent, unchecked steps; ~exp(-eps*H).
# │ Note: Hypothetical step accuracy, not a measured model property.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class HorizonCompounding:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ────────────────────────────────────────
    step_ok = 0.99  # hypothetical per-step probability of a correct step
    h_short, h_long = 10, 100  # horizons in turns
    target = 0.90  # task success rate to hold at the long horizon

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = 1 - step_ok
    p_short = step_ok**h_short
    p_long = step_ok**h_long
    eps_needed = 1 - target ** (1 / h_long)
    eps_ratio = eps / eps_needed
    eps_h_needed = eps_needed * h_long  # the product that sets reliability

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(p_long < 0.5 < target <= p_short, "Long horizon must fail most tasks; short must meet target")
    check(eps_needed < eps and eps_ratio > 5, "Holding the target must need a much lower step error")
    check(abs(eps_h_needed + math.log(target)) < 0.01, "eps*H must match -ln(target) in the small-eps limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    step_ok_str = fmt_percent(step_ok, style="prose")
    eps_str = fmt_percent(eps, style="prose")
    h_short_str, h_long_str = fmt_int(h_short), fmt_int(h_long)
    target_str = fmt_percent(target, style="prose")
    p_short_str = fmt_percent(p_short, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_long_str = fmt_percent(p_long, precision=1, style="prose")
    eps_needed_str = fmt_percent(eps_needed, precision=2, style="prose")
    eps_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eps_ratio, precision=1)
    p_short_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(step_ok, precision=2)}^{{{h_short}}} \approx {fmt(p_short, precision=3)}")
    p_long_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(step_ok, precision=2)}^{{{h_long}}} \approx {fmt(p_long, precision=3)}")
    eps_needed_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon = 1 - {fmt(target, precision=2)}^{{1/{h_long}}} \approx {fmt(eps_needed, precision=5)}")
    eps_h_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon H \approx {fmt(eps_h_needed, precision=3)}")
```

::: {#nbk-01-horizon-compounding .callout-notebook title="Horizon compounding"}

**Problem**: Each step of a repair agent is correct with probability `{python} HorizonCompounding.step_ok_str`, independently, and no step is checked before the next one builds on it. What fraction of tasks succeed at horizons of `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_short_str` and `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns, and what per-step error rate would hold the longer horizon at `{python} HorizonCompounding.target_str` success?

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_short_math`, so `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_short_str` of tasks succeed at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_short_str` turns, while `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_long_math` leaves `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_long_str` at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns. Holding `{python} HorizonCompounding.target_str` at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns requires `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_needed_math`, about `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_needed_str` per step and `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_ratio_mult_str` lower than the assumed `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_str`. For small $\epsilon$, $(1-\epsilon)^H \approx e^{-\epsilon H}$, and the requirement reads `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_h_math` at any horizon.

**Systems insight**: The product $\epsilon H$, not step accuracy alone, sets task reliability. A tenfold longer horizon demands a tenfold lower per-step error to hold the same success rate. The cheaper knob is usually the unchecked horizon itself: a check that rejects a bad step and retries it restarts the compounding, so a long task with reliable intermediate checks behaves like a chain of short unchecked segments. Supplying those checks is the job of the runtime, and @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure states the principle that assigns it.

:::

Checking converts a silent failure into a rejected attempt, and a rejected attempt still costs money. Suppose each attempt at a task is accepted with probability $p_{\text{acc}}$, independently of earlier attempts, and the runtime retries until one is accepted. The number of attempts is then geometric with mean $1/p_{\text{acc}}$. Each attempt costs $C_{\text{attempt}}$ in expectation, counting the tokens, tool time, verification, and review that a rejected attempt consumes as fully as an accepted one. The expected **cost per accepted task**\index{Cost per accepted task!definition} is therefore

$$C_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]}{p_{\text{acc}}}$$ {#eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task}

A deployed runtime bounds its retries, so some tasks end without acceptance. The cohort ratio in @sec-vol3-intro-fallacies measures the same quantity from recorded spend and acceptance counts, and @sec-vol3-agent-economics develops the full account. The form of @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task already shows which lever it rewards (notebook \ref{nbk-01-cost-per-accepted}).

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-intro-cost-per-accepted
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST PER ACCEPTED TASK: TOKEN PRICE VS. ACCEPTANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, @nbk-01-cost-per-accepted,
# │          @chk-vol3-intro-governance, and the accounting pitfall.
# │ Goal: Compare halving token prices with raising acceptance probability.
# │ Show: Baseline, both interventions, the break-even acceptance, and the
# │       understatement from charging only the accepted attempt.
# │ How:  C_eff = E[C_attempt] / p_acc with retry until acceptance.
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices and probabilities, not a provider schedule.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_pp, fmt_usd

class CostPerAccepted:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ────────────────────────────────────────
    c_model = 1.30  # scenario USD of model tokens per attempt
    c_other = 0.80  # scenario USD per attempt for sandbox, tests, and review
    p_acc = 0.40  # probability an attempt is accepted
    token_cut = 0.5  # fraction of token price removed by a cheaper tariff
    p_acc_better = 0.60  # acceptance after a context or tool improvement
    other_cut = 0.5  # checkpoint: fraction of sandbox/test/review cost removed
    p_acc_step = 0.10  # checkpoint: acceptance gain from a tool change

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    c_attempt = c_model + c_other
    token_share = c_model / c_attempt
    attempts = 1 / p_acc
    c_eff = c_attempt / p_acc
    c_attempt_cheap = c_model * (1 - token_cut) + c_other
    c_eff_cheap = c_attempt_cheap / p_acc
    c_eff_better = c_attempt / p_acc_better
    p_breakeven = p_acc / (1 - token_cut * token_share)
    gain_pp = round((p_breakeven - p_acc) * 100)  # whole points, for prose
    understate = c_eff / c_attempt  # accepted-attempt-only accounting error
    c_eff_ck_other = (c_model + c_other * (1 - other_cut)) / p_acc
    c_eff_ck_acc = c_attempt / (p_acc + p_acc_step)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(c_eff_better < c_eff_cheap < c_eff, "Raising acceptance must beat the token cut here")
    check(p_acc < p_breakeven < p_acc_better, "Break-even acceptance must lie between the two rates")
    check(abs(p_breakeven - c_attempt / c_eff_cheap) < 1e-9, "Break-even forms must agree")
    check(abs(c_eff_ck_other - c_eff_ck_acc) / c_eff < 0.05, "Checkpoint options must be a close call")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    c_model_str = fmt_usd(c_model, precision=2)
    c_other_str = fmt_usd(c_other, precision=2)
    c_attempt_str = fmt_usd(c_attempt, precision=2)
    c_attempt_cheap_str = fmt_usd(c_attempt_cheap, precision=2)
    p_acc_str = fmt_percent(p_acc, style="prose")
    p_acc_better_str = fmt_percent(p_acc_better, style="prose")
    p_breakeven_str = fmt_percent(round(p_breakeven, 2), style="prose")
    token_share_str = fmt_percent(round(token_share, 2), style="prose")
    gain_pp_str = fmt_pp(gain_pp, precision=0)
    p_acc_step_pp_str = fmt_pp(p_acc_step * 100, precision=0)
    attempts_str = fmt(attempts, precision=1)
    c_eff_str = fmt_usd(c_eff, precision=2)
    understate_mult_str = fmt_multiple(understate, precision=1)
    c_eff_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} = {fmt(c_eff, precision=2)}")
    c_eff_cheap_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt_cheap, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} \approx {fmt(c_eff_cheap, precision=2)}")
    c_eff_better_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc_better, precision=2)} = {fmt(c_eff_better, precision=2)}")
    p_breakeven_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} / (1 - {fmt(token_cut, precision=1)} \times {fmt(token_share, precision=2)}) \approx {fmt(p_breakeven, precision=2)}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-01-cost-per-accepted .callout-notebook title="Cheaper tokens or more acceptances"}

**Problem**: An attempt at the repair task spends `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_model_str` on model tokens and `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str` on the sandbox, tests, and review, and is accepted with probability `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str`. Which lowers cost per accepted task more: halving the token price, or raising acceptance to `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_better_str` through a context or tool improvement?

**Math**: The baseline attempt costs `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_str`, and the task needs `{python} CostPerAccepted.attempts_str` attempts on average, so @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task gives `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_math` dollars per accepted task. Halving the token price lowers the attempt to `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_cheap_str`, giving `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_cheap_math` dollars. Raising acceptance at the original attempt cost gives `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_better_math` dollars. Tokens are `{python} CostPerAccepted.token_share_str` of the attempt, so the price cut matches an acceptance of `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_breakeven_math`.

**Systems insight**: Cost per accepted task is inversely proportional to acceptance but only linear in each component's price. Halving the token price removes half of the tokens' `{python} CostPerAccepted.token_share_str` share, which is worth about as much as `{python} CostPerAccepted.gain_pp_str` of acceptance (`{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str` to `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_breakeven_str`); any context or tool change that lifts acceptance further beats the price cut, because acceptance divides the environment and verification spend as well. Compare interventions by their effect on $C_{\text{eff}}$ under the same acceptance contract, never by the price of a token.

:::

These two equations are the arithmetic the rest of the book returns to. @Eq-vol3-horizon-compounding says how fast reliability decays when steps go unchecked, and @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task says what a mechanism is worth: a check, a boundary, or a cache earns its place when it lowers $\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]$ by a larger factor than it lowers $p_{\text{acc}}$, or raises $p_{\text{acc}}$ by a larger factor than it raises the cost of each attempt.

Both relations take for granted two things the model cannot supply. Cost per accepted task needs a definition of acceptance, and restarting the compounding needs checks that can reject a step before the next one builds on it. The task contract supplies the first, and invariant closure the second.

## Governing Autonomous Execution {#sec-vol3-intro-governance}

The instruction "repair the race condition" leaves consequential decisions unstated. A proposed patch might remove synchronization and pass a sequential test while worsening the concurrent failure. A cleanup command might remove temporary files in a disposable workspace or delete the only copy of unfinished work. The goal alone does not distinguish these cases. Before the runtime admits an action, the task needs an explicit agreement about what may change and what evidence will justify accepting the result.

### The five-part task specification contract {#sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract}

A task specification makes delegated intent usable by the system around the model. It takes the form of a five-part contract, $\mathcal{C} = (G, \mathcal{E}_{\text{env}}, \mathcal{A}_{\text{perm}}, \mathcal{O}_{\text{avail}}, \mathcal{K}_{\text{comp}})$, whose components separate the desired outcome from the environment, permissions, observations, and acceptance criteria. The separation matters because an instruction can state an intention while supplying neither permission to act nor a means to determine whether the intention was met.

::: {#dfn-vol3-task-contract .callout-definition title="Task contract"}

***Task contract***\index{Task contract!definition} is the explicit specification of a delegated task that separates its goal, environment, permitted actions, available observations, and completion criteria, so that the runtime, not the model, decides what may execute and when the task is done.

1.  **Significance**: The completion criteria define what counts as accepted, which fixes the denominator of cost per accepted task. Two systems, or two versions of one system, can be compared only under the same contract.
2.  **Distinction**: A prompt communicates intent to the model; a contract is enforced by the runtime and the tool environment. The same sentence can appear in both, but only the contract constrains what executes.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Writing the permitted actions into the prompt alone. The model reads the limit, and the host process still allows everything its credentials allow.

:::

For the repair task, the goal $G$ carries a **negative scope**\index{Negative scope!definition}, the behavior the task must leave unchanged: here, everything outside the reported defect. The environment $\mathcal{E}_{\text{env}}$ identifies the source baseline and the workspace in which the patch will run. Permitted actions $\mathcal{A}_{\text{perm}}$ allow inspection, bounded edits, and test execution without granting access to unrelated files or permission to deploy. Available observations $\mathcal{O}_{\text{avail}}$ include source excerpts, test results, and the resulting diff. Completion criteria $\mathcal{K}_{\text{comp}}$ specify which checks the patch must pass and who must review aspects those checks do not cover. @Tbl-contract-template makes the five components concrete without committing them to a particular runtime implementation.

| Contract Component         |        Formal Symbol         | Systems Role                                        | Concrete Engineering Artifact                    |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| **Goal**                   |             $G$              | Desired end state and explicit negative scope       | Repair request that preserves unrelated behavior |
| **Environment**            |  $\mathcal{E}_{\text{env}}$  | Target state and execution conditions               | Source baseline and designated working copy      |
| **Permitted Actions**      | $\mathcal{A}_{\text{perm}}$  | Operations and resources within delegated authority | Allowed edit paths and test commands             |
| **Available Observations** | $\mathcal{O}_{\text{avail}}$ | Information the task may obtain and return          | Source excerpts, bounded test output, and diff   |
| **Completion Criteria**    | $\mathcal{K}_{\text{comp}}$  | Evidence and decision rule for accepting the result | Required regression checks and review decision   |
: **Five-Part Task Specification Contract**: Each component answers a different question about the repair task. A goal does not grant authority, and an allowed action does not establish completion. {#tbl-contract-template tbl-colwidths="[20,18,30,32]"}

Each component earns its place through the failure its absence permits. Without a negative scope in the goal, a patch can make the reported symptom disappear by removing the synchronization or the failing assertion. Without a designated environment, edits and installed dependencies can reach shared state, and no one can reproduce the result that was checked. Without an explicit action grant, dispatch inherits whatever the host process can do, as in @lst-vol3-naive-agent-loop. Without bounded observations, one unrestricted search can fill the next call's context. Without completion criteria, the model's own report becomes the only signal to stop.

A changing environment is allowed when the contract identifies which observations describe which state and which changes lie outside the task's control; a diagnostic task on a live service works this way. An observation limit must likewise distinguish an empty result from an incomplete one. When the runtime returns part of a test log, the next model call is told that output was omitted, because absence from the prompt is not evidence that an event never occurred.

Resource limits and stopping rules accompany the five-part specification. A task needs a turn or time limit, a spending boundary where applicable, and a defined response to exhausted resources or missing evidence. A stop on an exhausted budget is an unresolved outcome: the runtime returns the incomplete patch, records the unresolved check, and requests a human decision.

Writing the contract also reveals what is not yet delegable. "Improve maintainability" remains a judgment even in a structured field, so the task owner supplies an operational criterion, designates a qualified reviewer, or keeps that decision outside autonomous execution. The contract's job is to make such limits explicit where the runtime can act on them.

Later chapters implement each component. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling defines the permitted actions and the observations they return, @sec-vol3-sandboxes establishes the environment in which actions execute, @sec-vol3-agent-harness holds the goal, limits, and stopping rules for the running task, and @sec-vol3-evaluation develops the evidence that completion criteria require.

### The H·S·A exposure space {#sec-vol3-intro-hsa}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with no axis lit and the origin dot highlighted, marking a single model call."}

*Agents depart from a single model call along horizon, state, and authority.*
:::

A contract defines what the task should accomplish and the limits within which it may proceed. The infrastructure needed to support that contract depends on what can go wrong during execution. An isolated model call reads a supplied context and returns a proposal. Extending it into a trajectory introduces exposure through the length of execution, the state carried along it, and the actions the system can take. The book names these three exposures Horizon, State, and Authority, or H·S·A.

::: {#dfn-vol3-hsa-exposure-space .callout-definition title="H·S·A exposure space"}

***H·S·A exposure space***\index{HSA exposure space@H·S·A exposure space!definition} is the three-dimensional description of how far a delegated task departs from a single model call: its horizon $H$ in sequential turns, the state $S_0$ to $S_3$ it carries between calls, and the authority $A_0$ to $A_3$ it holds over its environment.

1.  **Significance**: Each axis names a quantity the runtime must bound. Horizon sets how far unchecked errors compound, state sets how many tokens and bytes each turn carries forward, and authority sets how much one wrong action can cost. Part II of the book closes state, Part III authority, and Part IV horizon.
2.  **Distinction**: A position in the space describes exposure, not an architecture. Closure, the set of bounds and evidence the runtime supplies in response, is not a fourth axis.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reading authority from a command's name. The level follows the operation's consequence in its environment, so the same delete can be $A_1$ in a disposable copy and $A_3$ against the only copy.

:::

Horizon $H$ counts sequential turns. A longer trajectory creates more opportunities for failed proposals, stale observations, and interruption, and @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding measures how quickly unchecked errors compound with it. Turns and elapsed time are separate budgets: a short sequence containing a slow external operation can outlast many local calls, so the runtime bounds both whenever either can constrain the task.

State $S$ describes what persists beyond one call. At $S_0$, no task state carries across calls. At $S_1$, the system carries conversational working state, including the context and any serving state the inference system retains between calls, such as the cached attention keys and values of earlier tokens. At $S_2$, it also maintains task-local working artifacts, such as an isolated source tree. At $S_3$, it depends on durable state that outlives the session or is authoritative beyond the working copy, such as a shared repository or database. A task can use several of these at once. The level identifies what must be preserved, refreshed, or protected, and which copy is authoritative when two disagree.

Authority $A$ describes the actions granted to the task. At $A_0$, access is read-only, although the information read can still leak through an output. At $A_1$, mutations remain inside a disposable workspace. At $A_2$, actions affect external systems but have a defined safe retry or compensating operation under stated conditions. At $A_3$, an action can produce an external consequence for which no adequate reversal is available. The level follows the operation's consequence in its environment rather than the command's name, and it describes the task's operational scope rather than the model's privileges. Under zero ambient authority, the runtime mediates each action against the task's current grant, so narrowing that grant is usually the cheapest protection, applied before any machinery is added around it.

The categories in @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy provide a common vocabulary for comparing tasks. They work as an engineering lens: two workloads in the same cell can still require different controls because the value of their data, the reliability of their tools, or the consequences of an error differ. A task can also change cells while its model and horizon stay fixed, as example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident} shows.

::: {#fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The H·S·A Exposure Space**: Horizon ($H$, turns), carried state ($S_0$ to $S_3$), and authority ($A_0$ to $A_3$) describe different departures from an isolated model call. The plotted positions and closure mechanisms are illustrative task configurations, not fixed properties of each workload class or unique design prescriptions. The task contract and failure consequences determine the required controls. Closure is the response to these exposures, not a fourth axis." fig-alt="Three-axis diagram with authority on the vertical axis from A0 read access to A3 irreversible external action, horizon in turns on the horizontal axis from H equals 1 to H at least 1,000, and state on a diagonal depth axis from S0 stateless to S3 durable shared state. Four workload cards are placed in the space, showing the support, remediation, repair, and research agents."}
![](images/svg/hsa_taxonomy.svg)
:::

::: {#exmp-01-hsa-incident .callout-example title="A working copy and the only copy"}

**Scenario**: A coding assistant must repair a defect while preserving unrelated source edits. Compare an isolated, disposable copy of the project with direct access to the author's sole authoritative workspace. The model, goal, and expected number of turns remain unchanged. In both cases, the assistant proposes deleting files while cleaning up its work.

**Diagnosis**: In the disposable copy, the working artifacts are $S_2$ state and the intended mutation authority is $A_1$. Discarding the copy can remove the candidate changes without damaging the original. In the authoritative workspace, the same command reaches $S_3$ state. If the files have an adequate recoverable version, the consequence differs from deleting unique, unrecorded edits; the latter crosses into $A_3$. Version control alone does not establish which case holds. The safer contract grants access only to the copy, excludes unrelated edits, and reserves transfer of the reviewed patch for a separate decision. The runtime must enforce that scope through tool access, not through a request that the model avoid mistakes.

**Systems lesson**: The failure boundary changed even though the model and horizon did not. Tests on the repaired code address behavior; a review of the diff against the preserved baseline addresses what changed. Neither substitutes for preventing the cleanup command from reaching the original workspace.

:::

### Four lighthouse workloads {#sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses}

The four cards in @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy mark the book's **lighthouses**\index{Lighthouse workload!definition}, four recurring workloads chosen because a different exposure binds each one, so a mechanism that decides one workload's cost can be irrelevant to another's. The repair agent is the running example throughout; the other three return wherever the repair agent cannot exercise a chapter's constraint.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-intro-lighthouse-roster
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LIGHTHOUSE ROSTER: REPAIR AGENT REGISTRY ANCHOR (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The four lighthouse callouts after @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy.
# │ Goal: Anchor the repair agent, the running example, to its registry profile,
# │       and pin the other three callouts' horizon words to their profiles.
# │ Show: Step budget and context window of the reference repair harness.
# │ How:  Read Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner; guard the research, remediation,
# │       and support horizons (Agents.Research/Remediation/Support) against
# │       the callouts' "tens of turns" and "a few turns" wording.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Agents
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int

class LighthouseRoster:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    repair = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner  # reference repository-repair harness
    research = Agents.Research.OrchestratorWorker
    remediation = Agents.Remediation.OnCall
    support = Agents.Support.CustomerOps

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    repair_steps = repair.max_trajectory_steps
    repair_window = repair.context_window.to("token").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(10 <= repair_steps <= 100, "Repair budget must sit in the tens-of-turns regime")
    check(repair_window >= 32_000, "Repair window must hold a multi-file working context")
    check(10 <= research.horizon_turns < 100, "Research callout says tens of turns per question")
    check(10 <= remediation.horizon_turns < 100, "Remediation callout says a moderate horizon of tens of turns")
    check(support.horizon_turns < 10, "Support callout says short sessions of a few turns")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    repair_steps_str = fmt_int(repair_steps)
    repair_window_str = fmt_int(repair_window)
```

::: {#lhs-vol3-repair-agent .callout-lighthouse title="Repair agent (long-horizon worker)"}

**Workload**: A repository coding agent repairs a reported defect in an isolated working copy and submits a patch for review. The connection-pool race condition in this chapter is its running instance, and the reference harness behind its numbers budgets `{python} LighthouseRoster.repair_steps_str` steps inside a `{python} LighthouseRoster.repair_window_str`-token context window.

**Exposure**: Long horizon (tens to hundreds of turns), a task-local working copy ($S_2$), and edits confined to that disposable workspace ($A_1$) until the reviewed patch leaves it.

**Binding constraint**: Errors compound over the horizon, and the context re-read on every turn grows with it. Re-reading accumulated input dominates its cost, and tests the agent cannot edit carry its acceptance.

:::

::: {#lhs-vol3-research-agent .callout-lighthouse title="Research agent (untrusted reader)"}

**Workload**: A browsing and deep-research agent answers a question by searching, reading, and synthesizing many external sources, often by fanning the work out to parallel workers.

**Exposure**: Horizons from tens of turns for one question to thousands for a standing crawl, a growing store of what it has read ($S_3$), and read access only ($A_0$).

**Binding constraint**: Everything it reads is untrusted input that can steer its later actions or leak through its output, so read access is still exposure. Retrieved and worker tokens dominate its cost, and fan-out multiplies them.

:::

::: {#lhs-vol3-remediation-agent .callout-lighthouse title="Remediation agent (irreversible actor)"}

**Workload**: An on-call agent diagnoses a production alert and changes live configuration or capacity to restore service. @Sec-vol3-conclusion follows one such task end to end.

**Exposure**: A moderate horizon (tens of turns), durable shared production state ($S_3$), and actions without an adequate reversal ($A_3$).

**Binding constraint**: One committed action can cost more than every token in the trajectory. Human approval latency and the expected loss from a wrong action dominate, which is why approval, compensation, and a point of no return are designed before the loop runs.

:::

::: {#lhs-vol3-support-agent .callout-lighthouse title="Support agent (interactive responder)"}

**Workload**: A customer-operations agent answers policy questions and issues refunds or bookings against a customer record while the customer waits. @Fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy plots its read-only configuration.

**Exposure**: Short sessions of a few turns each but many sessions at once, context plus the customer record ($S_1$ with $S_3$), and authority that rises from read-only answers ($A_0$) to refunds and bookings ($A_2$ to $A_3$) once the grant includes them.

**Binding constraint**: Response latency under concurrency, and answers grounded in the actual policy rather than a plausible one. Serving capacity and the state retained across many simultaneous sessions dominate its cost.

:::

Read together, the four lighthouses show why the book never ranks mechanisms in the abstract. Summarizing old context is central for the repair agent and marginal for a three-turn support session; holding each action for human approval is central for the remediation agent and pure overhead for a read-only researcher. Each later chapter names the lighthouse whose binding constraint its mechanism addresses.

### The invariant closure principle {#sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure}

The working-copy comparison in example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident} separates preventing an unwanted action from deciding whether a wanted result is good enough. A filesystem boundary prevents writes outside the assigned workspace. Whether a patch inside the workspace repairs a race condition is a second claim, and it needs evidence about the program's behavior. **Invariant closure**\index{Invariant closure!definition} assigns both responsibilities to mechanisms around the model rather than to the model's assurance that it complied.

::: {#pri-invariant-closure .callout-principle title="Invariant closure"}

**Invariant**: Constraints never rest on the model; bounds close mechanically below it, acceptance on evidence above it. Each enforced bound names the property and assumptions under which it holds, and each acceptance decision names the evidence standard it applies. Without either, a trajectory of $H$ steps, each correct with probability $1-\epsilon$, succeeds only with probability
$$ \Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\epsilon)^{H} $$
while a bound or a check turns a violating step into a rejected attempt instead.

**Implication**: Unchecked reliability decays exponentially with horizon, so it cannot be recovered by a more capable model alone. The runtime mediates permitted effects and resource use independently of the model's compliance. It accepts completion only when evidence meets the task contract, preserving the distinction between a passing check and a guarantee beyond that check's coverage. The contract itself is adopted by authorized people: the model can draft it but cannot adopt, relax, or certify against it. Greater operational exposure requires stronger justification for both the boundaries and the evidence.

:::

Mechanical enforcement establishes a particular boundary. A write restriction excludes protected paths provided every write passes through the enforcing mechanism and its isolation assumptions hold; it governs where writes land, and the correctness of the allowed files is a separate question. Validating the syntax of a tool request likewise establishes well-formedness, and authorization is a separate check. The design rule is to keep each enforced property narrower than the full task claim and to name it.

Evidence supports the acceptance decision at several **closure evidence levels**\index{Closure evidence levels!definition}. A model's self-report states what it claims to have accomplished; it is a claim, not an observation of the result. The end-to-end argument supplies the systems reason [@saltzer1984endtoend]: a property of the complete task can be established only by a check at an endpoint that knows what the task requires, so the correct operation of a lower layer, including fluent generation, cannot certify it. Static checks establish selected properties without running the task. **Visible tests**\index{Visible test!definition} exercise cases the agent can inspect, which makes them useful for diagnosis and also exposes the examples a candidate can be fitted to. **Sealed tests**\index{Sealed test!definition} withhold their cases and protect the checks from modification, which removes that opportunity and leaves their coverage unchanged. Formal proof establishes a specified property under an explicit model and assumptions, while whether the specification captures the user's intent remains a human judgment. The levels describe the basis of a claim rather than a strict ranking: a thorough sealed suite can support more than a proof of the wrong property.

For the race-condition repair, passing a sequential test supplies evidence about the sequential case. Keeping that test sealed prevents the agent from editing or inspecting it, and it remains a sequential test. Exercising the relevant concurrent behavior adds evidence for the reported defect, and review covers assumptions the tests leave open. A deterministic verdict can be repeatable and still incomplete, so acceptance claims stay within what the system measured.

Some criteria require judgment rather than a complete executable predicate. An evaluator assesses those against a stated rubric, recording the uncertainty and who holds the decision, while the mechanical permission checks continue to apply. When the available evidence cannot meet the contract, the system returns an unresolved outcome or escalates; a plausible explanation is never promoted to successful completion. @Sec-vol3-evaluation quantifies how reliable each kind of check is. Checks inside the trajectory also restart the compounding of @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, so the closure a task needs grows with its horizon.

### Workflows vs. model-directed loops {#sec-vol3-intro-workflow-vs-loop}

The repair task contains both predictable operations and choices that depend on new evidence. Preparing a working copy and running designated checks can follow a **fixed workflow**\index{Fixed workflow!definition}, whose control policy is specified in advance. Diagnosing an intermittent failure may require choosing the next file to inspect or hypothesis to test from observations that were unavailable at the start. A **model-directed loop**\index{Model-directed loop!definition}, in which the model chooses the next step from the latest observations, is useful at those decision points when its measured benefit justifies the added calls and uncertainty.

A fixed workflow can still branch, retry, and respond to changing inputs; what defines it is the policy fixed in advance. Model calls inside it still vary, so fixed control flow guarantees neither a deterministic result nor a particular latency. The two architectures are compared under the same task contract and evidence standard, and by @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task the loop wins where it raises acceptance by a larger factor than its added calls raise the cost of each attempt.

Approval is a separate decision from who chooses the next step. A fixed workflow can require human approval before an external effect, and a model-directed diagnostic loop can remain confined to a disposable copy. The runtime allows exploration within the granted scope while withholding deployment or another consequential action. A request for permission is only a request, and an approval covers the decision to act, not the effect's later success.

::: {#chk-vol3-intro-governance .callout-checkpoint title="Changing the task boundary"}

A repair agent can inspect and edit a disposable working copy and return a patch for review. Its contract grants no access to the deployment service.

**Reading the boundary**

- [ ] **Authority**: The task now includes deployment. Which authority level does it move to, and which permission decision must be added that no passing test can supply?
- [ ] **State**: The workspace turns out to hold the only copy of unrelated edits. Which exposure changes, and which single change to the grant removes it?
- [ ] **Acceptance evidence**: A sealed sequential test passes after the race-condition repair. Which claim does it support, and what further evidence would you require before accepting?
- [ ] **Control policy**: Which steps of the repair would you assign to a fixed workflow, and which decision must stay model-directed?

**Pricing the choice**

- [ ] **Cost per accepted task estimate**: An attempt costs `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_str`, of which `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str` is sandbox, tests, and review, and `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str` of attempts are accepted. Estimate the cost per accepted task if you halve that `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str`, and again if a tool change raises acceptance by `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_step_pp_str`. Which would you fund?

:::

The contract determines what the system owes the task, and H·S·A exposes where its execution needs protection; either control policy inherits both obligations. The architecture must assign an owner to assembling information, proposing actions, enforcing their scope, preserving the task's state, and deciding whether the accumulated evidence meets the contract.

## The Agentic System Architecture {#sec-vol3-intro-stochastic-computer}

In the repair task, the same proposed patch can lead to different outcomes depending on the system around the model. One runtime may apply it to the permitted working copy, preserve the original test fixtures, and return the compiler's diagnostic. Another may apply it to the wrong repository or lose the diagnostic when a process exits. The task contract describes the required behavior; the architecture assigns responsibility for carrying it out.

The *stochastic computer*\index{Stochastic computer} provides a compact map of these responsibilities. The foundation model supplies learned computation, corresponding loosely to a processor; context and persistent stores supply memory; tools provide input and output; and the runtime coordinates execution, in the role an operating system occupies in a conventional computer. Learning from trajectories changes future model behavior, while coordination connects agents and distributes work. The correspondence orients rather than specifies, and the places where it breaks are the instructive ones: a model proposal is a request the runtime may refuse, unlike an instruction, and an assembled context is a selected copy, while the environment holds the authoritative record. Those two breaks determine the interfaces between the actual components.

@Fig-vol3-agentic-architecture places the runtime between proposals and tool effects and returns observations to the same decision owner. Evaluation uses the resulting task records; learning and coordination extend this structure without replacing its control boundaries.

::: {#fig-vol3-agentic-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Agentic System Responsibilities**: The live loop separates context, model proposals, authorized tool execution, and observations from the environment. The task contract governs the runtime's acceptance decision. Task records support evaluation; dashed paths mark optional learning and coordination extensions, not prerequisites for every delegated task." fig-alt="A task contract points to an agent runtime. The runtime selects information from agent memory, which supplies context to a foundation model. Model proposals return to the runtime, which sends authorized actions to tools. Tools affect an environment that returns observations and evidence. Below, task records flow to evaluation; dashed arrows lead to trajectory learning and coordination."}
![](images/svg/agentic_systems_architecture.svg)
:::

### Responsibilities in the live loop {#sec-vol3-intro-live-loop}

The model receives the task description, relevant source material, and observations selected for the current call. It returns a proposal, such as a request to inspect the connection-pool implementation or a candidate patch. The proposal can be useful without being correct, well formed, or permitted. Model invocation therefore ends at an interface where the runtime can inspect the output before allowing any tool to act on it.

That interface depends on what the model was shown. Agent memory supplies the current context and retains information needed later, but these jobs have different lifetimes. The next call may need only the affected function and a concise compiler diagnostic. The complete diagnostic can remain outside the context, available for later inspection, while the repository remains the source of the current file contents. The serving system may also retain intermediate attention computations to avoid repeating work. Losing that derived computation need not lose the task record or undo a file edit. Separating these objects prevents a performance decision about retained computation from becoming an accidental decision about which facts survive.

Tools connect proposals to the environment. A file-reading tool returns an observation; a patching tool changes the working copy; a test runner produces evidence about the changed program. Their interfaces specify the arguments accepted and the results returned. Authorization decides whether a particular invocation falls within the task's permitted scope. A sandbox bounds the resources and environment that executing code can reach. These responsibilities complement one another. A permitted command can still contain faulty code, and a contained command can still perform the wrong operation on a file it is allowed to modify.

The agent runtime coordinates these components across the trajectory. It owns the execution record containing the task's limits, pending work, completed operations, and acceptance decisions. It selects when to call the model, mediates proposed tool use, records observations, and decides whether to continue, wait, stop, or escalate under the contract. The record must distinguish what the model proposed from what the environment reports actually happened: dispatch is not success, and silence is not the absence of an effect.

The four responsibilities can share one program in a small application or spread across services in a large deployment; the separation that matters concerns authority and evidence. Permissions come only from the runtime's grant, acceptance criteria only from the contract, and the execution record only from the runtime's observations, never from model-visible text, a tool response, or a model's completion claim.

### The six-phase turn execution lifecycle {#sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle}

Consider the turn in which the repair agent proposes changing the mutex acquisition logic. Before the proposal can become an accepted repair, it passes through decisions owned by different components. A useful decomposition separates six phases:

1. The runtime assembles the next context from the task contract, current working state, and relevant observations. It checks whether the remaining resources permit another call and includes enough evidence to distinguish the current workspace from earlier versions.
2. The model reads that context and returns a proposal together with the invocation's completion status. A partial response or failed call is not a complete tool request. The runtime retains the distinction before attempting to interpret the output.
3. The runtime validates the proposed operation against the tool interface and the task's authority. For the patch, this includes checking the target workspace and allowed files. It rejects invalid requests or waits for required approval before dispatching an effect.
4. The tool executes the authorized operation within its assigned limits. Applying a patch changes the working copy, even though the repair has not yet passed its tests. The runtime tracks outstanding work rather than treating dispatch as completion.
5. The runtime records the tool's observation and obtains the evidence needed for the next decision. A compiler error reports a failed build; passing tests report success on the cases executed. Missing or incomplete results remain explicitly unresolved rather than becoming evidence of success.
6. The runtime assesses progress against the task contract. It may authorize another turn, wait for outstanding work, request clarification, stop without acceptance, or accept the deliverable under the stated evidence standard. The decision includes the status of relevant external effects and the remaining resource limits, not merely the model's latest answer.

The phases expose responsibility boundaries rather than prescribe a universal scheduler. An authorized operation may wait for an external service, and a model response may be a candidate final answer rather than a tool call. Implementations can overlap independent work, but they cannot obtain authorization from an observation that arrives after the effect or infer an effect's outcome from a proposal alone. @Fig-vol3-ch01-execution-lifecycle draws these branches. A rejection enters the observation phase as feedback without reaching a tool, required approval and outstanding work pause the turn without ending it, and assessment either starts another turn, accepts the deliverable, or stops without acceptance.

::: {#fig-vol3-ch01-execution-lifecycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle**: Each phase marks a change in which component is responsible, not a mandated scheduler. The runtime assembles context, authorizes requests, records outcomes, and assesses progress; the model only proposes, and only an authorized request reaches a tool. A timed-out tool leaves its outcome unknown, and acceptance requires evidence independent of the model's own report, so exhausted limits end in an unresolved outcome or escalation rather than success." fig-alt="Six phase boxes arranged in a U. Top row, left to right: 1 context assembly, runtime; 2 model invocation, model; 3 validate and authorize, runtime. An authorized arrow descends to the bottom row, which runs right to left: 4 tool execution, tool; 5 observation and evidence, runtime; 6 assess against contract, runtime. A dashed rejected arrow runs from phase 3 to phase 5. Dashed arrows from phases 3 and 6 lead to a non-terminal wait box. An another-turn arrow returns from phase 6 to phase 1, and phase 6 also leads to an accept-deliverable box and a stop-without-acceptance box."}
![](images/svg/ch01_execution_lifecycle.svg)
:::

For the repair task, we can follow the resulting evidence without confusing the stages. Applying the patch establishes that the workspace changed. A successful build establishes that the checked program compiles. The regression tests add evidence about behavior. Acceptance depends on whether those results satisfy the agreed criteria for this repair. Recording each stage separately preserves both useful progress and the limits of what has been established.

### Resource costs of a turn {#sec-vol3-intro-accelerator-host}

Running the test suite can take longer than generating the patch that requested it. During that wait, the task remains active even though it needs no new model output. The runtime must retain enough state to interpret the result when it arrives, but it need not retain every temporary computation used by the previous model call. Conversely, discarding reusable model state may make the next call more expensive. The task's logical lifetime and the lifetime of resources allocated to one invocation are separate engineering choices. Retained serving state held idle while a slow tool runs is the **tool-wait problem**\index{Tool-wait problem!definition}; @sec-vol3-kv-cache quantifies whether to keep, move, or drop that state, and @sec-vol3-agent-economics prices the choice per accepted task.

The same distinction applies to context growth. Preserving a complete diagnostic for audit does not require sending every line to every subsequent call. Call latency, retained memory, tool time, and overall task cost must be measured separately before choosing what to keep, recompute, or summarize. Once each object has one owner and one lifetime, the measurements that decide its retention policy follow directly.

### Improvement beyond one trajectory {#sec-vol3-intro-across-task}

A repaired program supplies a deliverable; its trajectory supplies evidence about how the system reached it. Across tasks, those records reveal repeated failures and wasted work. Evaluation determines whether a change improves task outcomes under the same criteria. The change may affect context selection, tool interfaces, or runtime policy before it requires changing the model itself.

When model adaptation is justified, selected trajectories become training examples or environments for reward-based learning. The data must preserve the difference between model-authored proposals and environment-produced observations. A learned policy can become more likely to choose a useful action, but training does not grant additional authority or remove the need to check task completion. Evaluation must therefore precede learning and must test the resulting policy again before deployment.

Coordination introduces a different extension. Several agents may work on one task, or many independent tasks may share serving and execution resources. Delegation within a task occurs during live execution, not only in a separate offline layer. It creates additional obligations for shared state, returned evidence, and the permissions given to each participant. Whether delegation or additional infrastructure is worthwhile depends on its contribution to accepted outcomes after accounting for coordination, unsuccessful attempts, and resource costs.

The architecture thus connects a bounded live loop to optional paths for improving and scaling it. A task contract establishes the obligations, components own the corresponding decisions and records, and evaluation tests the assembled system. The curriculum follows those dependencies so that learning and coordination extend a system whose single-task behavior is already understood.

## Book Organization {#sec-vol3-intro-book-organization}

The repair task needs a model to propose a change, selected context to inform it, tools to apply it, and a runtime to decide whether execution may continue. Each responsibility raises a different engineering question. Improving the proposal does not establish permission to apply it, and containing its effects does not establish that the repair works. The book develops these responsibilities separately before combining them into a complete system.

### The causal curriculum spine {#sec-vol3-intro-causal-spine}

A model call provides the starting interface. Repeated calls produce working state, and tool interactions connect that state to an environment whose changes can outlast the call. The runtime must then supervise the whole trajectory and preserve enough evidence to assess its outcome. Only after that assessment can recorded trajectories support justified changes to the policy or the deployment. @Tbl-causal-spine maps this dependency sequence to the seven parts.

| Part                                   | Governing Problem                                                                      | New Capability                                                                                | Exposure Addressed                        |
|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| **Part I: The Model**                  | A fallible model proposal consumes time and resources.                                 | Interpret the call contract and decide when additional inference is worthwhile.               | None yet; the single call is the origin   |
| **Part II: Agent Memory**              | Growing histories compete for limited context and can contain stale information.       | Manage the next call's context, its serving state, and information retained across tasks.     | State                                     |
| **Part III: Tool Use**                 | Proposed actions need permission, containment, and protection against untrusted input. | Define tool interactions, bound execution, and constrain misuse of legitimate access.         | Authority                                 |
| **Part IV: The Agent Runtime**         | A sequence of permitted actions can still stall, lose state, or fail its task.         | Supervise execution, survive interruption, recover from failures, and evaluate outcomes.      | Horizon                                   |
| **Part V: Learning from Trajectories** | Execution records do not automatically constitute suitable learning data.              | Curate trajectories, teach demonstrated behavior, and improve policies using outcome rewards. | None; changes the model, not the exposure |
| **Part VI: Agents at Scale**           | Delegation and concurrency introduce coordination costs and shared resource limits.    | Compare multi-agent designs and provision resources per accepted task.                        | All three, multiplied                     |
| **Part VII: Synthesis**                | Component-level guarantees leave obligations at their interfaces.                      | Follow an incident-remediation task through the system and justify its acceptance.            | All three, together                       |
: **Causal Dependency Spine**: Each part develops capabilities that the later parts use to govern, evaluate, improve, and scale complete trajectories. The last column names the H·S·A exposure each part addresses. {#tbl-causal-spine tbl-colwidths="[20,30,30,20]"}

The chapters follow the same sequence. In Part I, @sec-vol3-foundation-model establishes what a call reads, returns, and costs, and @sec-vol3-test-time-compute decides when additional inference improves the selected result. Part II closes the state exposure. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering selects what each call sees, @sec-vol3-kv-cache prices the serving state that context occupies, and @sec-vol3-long-term-memory governs what persists across sessions. Part III closes the authority exposure. @Sec-vol3-tool-calling separates validation, authorization, dispatch, and evidence of effect, @sec-vol3-sandboxes bounds what executing code can reach, and @sec-vol3-security addresses untrusted input that steers legitimate access.

Part IV closes the horizon exposure. @Sec-vol3-agent-harness runs the loop under budgets and approvals, @sec-vol3-durable-execution preserves progress through interruption, @sec-vol3-failure-recovery repairs or compensates failed work, and @sec-vol3-evaluation measures the assembled system. Part V changes the model and moves no exposure. @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation prepares records for a learning use, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning teaches demonstrated behavior, and @sec-vol3-rlvr optimizes against verifiable rewards. Part VI multiplies all three exposures. @Sec-vol3-multi-agent divides a task among agents, and @sec-vol3-agent-economics prices and provisions the system per accepted task. @Sec-vol3-conclusion then follows one task through every boundary.

The same order governs how the book responds to a recurring failure. Changing what the model sees is cheap and undone by the next edit, while changing model weights is the most expensive and least reversible intervention, because it alters behavior on tasks the failure never touched. @Sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order orders the tool, schema, and runtime interventions between those extremes by cost and reversibility, as a default rather than a sequence every failure must climb.

Evaluation therefore appears before learning. A recorded action might have been permitted but unsuccessful; a successful final result might include an earlier failed attempt that taught the agent how to recover. The learning chapters need those distinctions to decide which records to retain and what behavior each record should teach. Similarly, coordination follows the complete single-agent system so that the value of additional agents can be compared against a capable baseline rather than an incomplete loop.

The order is a teaching dependency. A deployed system includes the mechanisms its exposure demands, so a short read-only task runs on far less than a long task that updates shared services. The conclusion applies the book's accumulated contracts to the remediation agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}): inspecting a latency alert, gathering diagnostic evidence, proposing a repair, obtaining required approval, and checking the resulting service behavior.
